html:
The Blemmyes were a nomadic people of the Eastern Desert between the Nile and the Red Sea, in today's southern Egypt and northern Sudan. They appear in written sources from the 600s BCE to the 700s CE, and on the map from 500 BCE to 700 CE.

They herded animals in the desert hills and controlled the routes to its gold and emerald mines and to the Red Sea ports. Greek and Roman writers told wild stories about them, even that they had faces on their chests, but they were real neighbours of Meroe and of Roman Egypt.

From the 200s CE they raided Upper Egypt. In 298 the Roman emperor Diocletian pulled the frontier back to the island of Philae and paid yearly subsidies to the Blemmyes and their neighbours, the Nobades, to keep the peace. Both peoples kept the right to worship the goddess Isis at Philae, one of the last places where the old Egyptian religion was practised, until Justinian closed the temple in the 530s.

By the late 300s the Blemmyes held parts of Lower Nubia and had kings of their own, known from inscriptions at Philae. In the 400s or 500s Silko, king of the Nobades, defeated them, and Lower Nubia became the Christian kingdom of Nobatia, later joined to Makuria.

Archaeologists link the Blemmyes with part of the "X-Group" culture of late Nubia, and most scholars see them as ancestors of the Beja, who still live in the same desert. They are one of the few peoples who appear in the records of Kush, Rome and Byzantium alike, as the desert power the river kingdoms had to deal with.
sum: The Blemmyes were a nomadic people of the Eastern Desert between the Nile and the Red Sea, in today's southern Egypt and northern Sudan. They appear in written sources from the 600s BCE to the 700s CE, and on the map from 500 BCE to 700 CE.
